    VMware patches vCenter zero-day exploited in attacks since September
    bleepingcomputer.com · 20 Nov 2026 00:26 UTC openai-codex / gpt-5.6-terra

    In plain words

    Broadcom released an urgent fix for a serious flaw in VMware vCenter, software companies use to manage large groups of virtual computers. Researchers say a suspected China-linked hacking group used the flaw since September to get into affected systems without a password, take administrator control, and steal sensitive information. Organizations using VMware vCenter and related VMware products are affected if they have not installed the updated versions, and the risk is especially serious because an intruder could gain control of many virtual machines from one central system.

    Summary
    Broadcom released an emergency patch for CVE-2026-123890, a critical VMware vCenter authentication-bypass flaw exploited since September by the suspected Chinese-linked Armory Castle group. Organizations should patch vCenter immediately, as exploitation can grant attackers administrative control of virtualized environments and enable credential theft.

    Broadcom released emergency updates on November 19 to address CVE-2026-123890, a critical authentication-bypass flaw in VMware vCenter Server’s Directory Service. The issue allows an unauthenticated attacker with network access to bypass login requirements and gain unauthorized access to a vulnerable vCenter Server. Successful compromise can provide administrative control over the virtual machines managed by the server. Broadcom said there are no official workarounds, although network restrictions and firewall controls can reduce exposure.

    Mandiant and Google Threat Intelligence Group reported that the suspected Chinese state-sponsored group Armory Castle exploited the flaw in attacks starting in early September 2026. The group reportedly used the BONESAW tool to create a vCenter SSO administrator account, steal the directory database, and extract SAML signing keys. It then used SAWSNAKE to forge authentication tokens, bypass multifactor authentication, and impersonate legitimate users, while deploying multiple web shells and backdoors for continued access. Broadcom urged organizations using affected vCenter, SDDC Manager, or VMware Tools for Windows versions to apply the security updates as soon as possible.

    • The same intrusion campaign reportedly combined a BeyondTrust Remote Support zero-day with the VMware vCenter flaw, allowing attackers to move from compromised remote-support appliances through internal Linux systems to VMware infrastructure.
    • By stealing SAML signing keys and using the SAWSNAKE tool, the attackers could forge login tokens, bypass multifactor authentication, and impersonate legitimate users after the initial vCenter compromise.
    • The issue affects vCenter whether or not Enhanced Linked Mode is enabled, so disabling or avoiding that configuration does not remove exposure.
    • Broadcom said that network restrictions and firewall controls may reduce exposure, but it provided no official workaround, making installation of the security updates the primary remediation.
    Key Points
    • 01Broadcom released emergency security updates on November 19 to fix CVE-2026-123890, a critical VMware vCenter Server authentication-bypass flaw.
    • 02The flaw lets an unauthenticated attacker with network access to a vulnerable vCenter Server gain unauthorized administrative access and control the virtual machines it manages.
    • 03Mandiant and Google Threat Intelligence Group reported that the suspected Chinese state-sponsored group Armory Castle exploited the flaw in attacks beginning in early September 2026.
    • 04The attackers used a custom Golang tool called BONESAW to create a vCenter Single Sign-On administrator account, steal the directory database, and extract SAML signing keys.
    • 05Broadcom said there are no official workarounds and urged organizations to install the patches as soon as possible.

In plain words

A suspected China-linked espionage group used a previously unknown flaw in VMware vCenter, software organizations use to manage virtual computers, to break in without a password and gain top-level control. The group then searched internal networks, stole files, created extra administrator accounts, and set up ways to return later. This matters because control of vCenter can give attackers broad access to an organization’s virtual systems and data, and the flaw was already being used before fixes became available.

Summary
China-linked Armory Castle exploited the critical VMware vCenter authentication-bypass zero-day CVE-2026-123890 to obtain administrator access, steal data, and persist across targeted environments. Organizations should urgently apply Broadcom’s November 2026 patches and investigate exposure to associated tools including BONESAW and SAWSNAKE.

The suspected China-linked espionage group Armory Castle, formerly UNC5221, exploited the critical VMware vCenter Server zero-day CVE-2026-123890 in early September 2026. The flaw is an unauthenticated authentication bypass in VMware Directory Service that can establish a session as administrator@vsphere.local. Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant said the group used a Golang utility called BONESAW to exploit the issue, obtain data such as the data.mdb database, take over the vCenter Security Token Service, and create an SSO administrator account. Broadcom released patches on November 19, 2026, including vCenter 8.0 U3m and designated Cloud Foundation and vSphere Foundation versions.

The vCenter activity was part of a wider campaign that also exploited a BeyondTrust Remote Support zero-day, then moved through an internal Linux appliance toward the virtualized environment. Armory Castle used tools including SLIMSAVAGE and CAGEMATCH web shells, the SAWSNAKE token-forging utility, and BEARBONES and LAZYBONES backdoors. The group scanned for VMware-related ports, enabled vCenter SSH through the VAMI API, created an additional administrator account, enumerated ESXi storage, and stole archived data through the compromised Remote Support appliance. Google said the use of two zero-days and specialized malware for several appliance types demonstrated substantial resources and a sustained effort against high-priority targets.

  • The intrusion moved from a compromised BeyondTrust Remote Support device through an internal Linux appliance and into the virtualized environment, showing that the vCenter compromise was part of a broader multi-system campaign rather than an isolated entry point.
  • After BONESAW accessed vCenter, SAWSNAKE could generate forged login tokens that let the attackers impersonate users and bypass multi-factor authentication through a Golden SAML technique.
  • The group specifically scanned for ports 9080, 5480, and 2012; port 2012 is the vCenter Single Sign-On control interface used in its remote exploitation workflow.
  • The attackers established several persistence paths on vCenter and ESXi systems, including a new administrator account, enabled SSH through the VAMI API, and an SSH public key placed in the root account’s authorized keys.
  • Google said the campaign’s use of two zero-days and several specialized toolsets targeting different appliances indicates substantial resources and operational commitment.
Key Points
  • 01Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant attributed early September 2026 exploitation of the critical VMware vCenter flaw CVE-2026-123890 to the suspected China-linked group Armory Castle, formerly UNC5221.
  • 02CVE-2026-123890 is an unauthenticated VMware Directory Service flaw that can create an authenticated administrator@vsphere.local session, enabling attackers to run commands and obtain files such as the data.mdb database.
  • 03Broadcom released fixes for the flaw on November 19, 2026, including VMware vCenter 8.0 U3m and specified VMware Cloud Foundation and vSphere Foundation releases.
  • 04Google observed the group using the Golang-based BONESAW utility to exploit the flaw, extract database data, take over the vCenter token service, and create an SSO administrator account.
  • 05The campaign also involved web shells, backdoors, internal scanning for VMware-related ports, ESXi file-system reconnaissance, and theft of archived data.

    nginx2root (CVE-2026-123007): HTTP/2 Flaw Lets Attackers Run Code on Unpatched nginx Servers
    stepsecurity.io · 20 Nov 2026 00:05 UTC openai-codex / gpt-5.6-terra
    TAGSaustraliacve-2026-123007cve-2026-123633f5germanyinteger-underflowirelandjapankubernetesnginxnginx2rootubuntuunited-kingdomunited-statesuse-after-free
    In plain words

    The article describes a serious flaw in many older nginx web servers, software used to run websites, that could let an outsider take control of a server without a password. It affects nginx installations using HTTP/2, including versions from 2015 through 1.31.8, although the published method needs a fast direct connection and other special conditions. Website operators should install the fixed update and restart the software, or temporarily turn off HTTP/2. The stakes are high because a successful attacker could run commands as the web server and potentially disrupt or alter the sites and services it hosts.

    Summary
    CVE-2026-123007 is a critical HTTP/2 flow-control flaw in nginx versions 1.9.5 through 1.31.8 that can enable unauthenticated remote code execution under specific conditions. Upgrade to nginx 1.31.9 or 1.30.7 (or your vendor’s backport) and restart nginx immediately; disable HTTP/2 if patching is not yet possible.

    CVE-2026-123007 is a critical nginx HTTP/2 flaw, disclosed as part of the nginx2root group of vulnerabilities and fixed in nginx 1.31.9 and 1.30.7. It affects nginx releases from 1.9.5 through 1.31.8 when HTTP/2 is enabled. The article reports that public researchers demonstrated remote code execution, including an exploit that can run commands as the nginx worker process without credentials under stated conditions.

    The issue stems from an accounting error in HTTP/2 response-data limits that can cause nginx to incorrectly accept excessive connection credit, eventually leading to memory corruption. The published full exploit requires a direct connection, approximately 119 GiB of traffic within nginx’s one-hour connection limit, an otherwise idle server, and an x86-64 CPU with AVX-512; a smaller proof of concept crashes workers without AVX-512. Organizations should upgrade to a fixed release or distribution backport and restart nginx, since a configuration reload does not replace the running binary; if they cannot patch immediately, they can disable HTTP/2, though this breaks gRPC through nginx and does not address the other nginx2root bugs.

    • A normal nginx configuration reload does not replace the vulnerable program code; administrators must restart nginx or use its on-the-fly binary upgrade mechanism after updating.
    • A reverse proxy that terminates HTTP/2 prevented the tested public exploit because it rebuilt the HTTP/2 responses, but the vulnerable backend still required patching.
    • External version scans and the nginx version string can be misleading because Linux distributions may backport the fix without changing the upstream nginx version number.
    • The public exploit could succeed again without restarting nginx after a worker crash because replacement workers inherited the master process's same memory layout.
    • The malicious HTTP/2 window-update messages do not appear in normal nginx access logs, so connection-level traffic data and worker crash logs are more useful for spotting attempts.
    Key Points
    • 01CVE-2026-123007 is an integer-underflow flaw in nginx HTTP/2 flow-control accounting that affects nginx versions 1.9.5 through 1.31.8 when HTTP/2 is enabled.
    • 02The flaw can corrupt memory and, under the published exploit’s stated conditions, allow an unauthenticated attacker to run a command as the nginx worker process.
    • 03nginx fixed the issue in versions 1.31.9 and 1.30.7, while Linux distributions may provide the fix through backported package updates.
    • 04The published full exploit requires a direct connection, roughly 119 GiB of traffic within nginx’s one-hour connection limit, an otherwise idle server, and an x86-64 CPU with AVX-512.
    • 05Organizations that cannot patch immediately can disable HTTP/2, although doing so breaks gRPC through nginx and does not address the other three nginx2root bugs.

    This is a critical patch for widely deployed nginx HTTP/2 servers, with a public exploit reported to achieve unauthenticated code execution as the nginx worker user. Although no exploitation in the wild was reported, affected organizations need to patch, restart nginx, or disable HTTP/2 promptly.

In plain words

Researchers disclosed five serious flaws in nginx, widely used software that runs websites and routes web traffic, which could let an unauthenticated stranger crash a server or potentially run commands on it. The greatest risk is to organizations whose nginx servers are directly reachable from the internet, while sites placed behind Cloudflare are protected from several of the most serious connection-based attacks only if their underlying servers cannot be reached directly. Because nginx is used on millions of systems and one related Linux flaw could give an intruder full control of a machine, affected organizations need to install fixes and restrict direct access quickly.

Summary
Five newly disclosed nginx2root flaws, especially CVE-2026-123007 in HTTP/2, can enable remote code execution on vulnerable nginx servers and should be patched immediately. Cloudflare-proxied origins are shielded from the HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 attack paths only if attackers cannot directly reach the origin, but resolver and mail-proxy configurations still require remediation.

F5 and nginx.org disclosed ten nginx vulnerabilities on November 18, 2026, including five memory-corruption flaws collectively called nginx2root. The flaws can allow an unauthenticated attacker to crash an nginx worker and, according to Xint’s research, potentially run commands as the nginx worker. CVE-2026-123007, affecting HTTP/2-enabled nginx releases since 2015, is presented as the most serious because HTTP/2 is commonly enabled and the bug can lead to an out-of-bounds memory read/write. Xint also identified a separate Linux SCTP kernel flaw that could reportedly elevate nginx-worker code execution to root access on the host, including from a Docker container.

Cloudflare states that its edge is not affected and that origins behind its HTTP proxy are shielded from the HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 flaws because client connections end at Cloudflare rather than reaching nginx directly. This protection does not apply if attackers can connect directly to an origin, nor does it fully protect the resolver flaw CVE-2026-123634 or the mail-proxy flaw CVE-2026-113425. Organizations are advised to update nginx Open Source to 1.30.7 or 1.31.9, nginx Plus to fixed 37.x releases, restart nginx after updating, and restrict origins so they are reachable only through Cloudflare. The article also recommends disabling unneeded HTTP/2, HTTP/3, mail-proxy, and SCTP functionality as temporary mitigations where patching is delayed.

  • Cloudflare’s protection is based on ending and recreating web connections at its edge, not on a WAF signature, so attacker-controlled HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 control messages never reach a properly isolated nginx origin.
  • The known CVE-2026-123007 attack path requires unusually large traffic volumes—about 128 GB in Rapid7’s proof of concept—over one long-lived HTTP/2 connection, creating a potentially visible pattern of massive inbound traffic with little response traffic.
  • A configuration reload does not replace nginx’s running program, so organizations must restart nginx or complete a binary upgrade after installing a fixed package.
  • The related Linux SCTP flaw can reportedly turn code execution as an nginx worker into root access on the host, including from an nginx container, and systems that do not use SCTP can block automatic loading of its kernel module as a temporary safeguard.
  • Package version output alone may be misleading because Linux distributions can backport fixes without changing nginx’s reported upstream version, so administrators need to compare full package versions with their distribution’s advisory.
Key Points
  • 01F5 and nginx.org disclosed five nginx2root memory-corruption vulnerabilities on November 18, 2026, including CVE-2026-123007, an HTTP/2 flaw affecting nginx releases since 1.9.5.
  • 02CVE-2026-123007 can be triggered when HTTP/2 is enabled and, according to the cited research, may allow an unauthenticated attacker to crash an nginx worker or run commands after bypassing address randomization protections.
  • 03Cloudflare says its HTTP proxy protects proxied origins from the HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 nginx2root attacks because client connections terminate at Cloudflare’s edge, but this protection does not apply when an attacker can reach the origin directly.
  • 04The resolver flaw CVE-2026-123634 and the mail-proxy flaw CVE-2026-113425 are not fully protected by Cloudflare’s HTTP proxy and require affected nginx configurations to be patched or restricted.
  • 05Organizations should update to nginx Open Source 1.30.7 or 1.31.9, nginx Plus 37.0.8.1 or 37.3.0.1, or a vendor-provided fixed build, then restart nginx.
OPEN SOURCE ↗
JUSTIFICATION

This is a critical patch event for widely deployed nginx: five disclosed memory-corruption flaws may enable unauthenticated crashes or code execution, with HTTP/2-enabled deployments broadly exposed. The article also provides concrete fixed versions, affected configurations, mitigations, and important limits on Cloudflare proxy protection.

In plain words

Hackers used a serious flaw in Cisco Expressway, a system organizations use for communications, to take control of four devices at a Russian organization. After gaining control, they explored the organization’s internal network and looked for shared files, databases, remote computer access, and stored credentials. The incident shows that an exposed internet-facing device can give criminals a route into more sensitive parts of an organization, making prompt software updates, network separation, and monitoring important.

Summary
Attackers exploited the critical Cisco Expressway flaw CVE-2026-76466 shortly after a public PoC was released, gaining root access to internet-facing devices and pivoting into a Russian organization’s internal network. Organizations should urgently patch or migrate affected Expressway versions and investigate for the published indicators of compromise.

Threat actors exploited CVE-2026-76466, a critical Cisco Expressway flaw with a CVSS score of 9.8, to compromise a Russian organization. The vulnerability can allow an unauthenticated remote attacker with network access to execute operating-system commands as root on an affected device. Cisco said the issue involves persistent cookies and insufficient validation of client certificates when clustering TLS Verify Mode is enabled.

F6 reported that attackers exploited Cisco Expressway X15.5.3 devices after a public proof-of-concept exploit became available, initially compromising two internet-facing devices and reaching two additional internal cluster nodes through one of them. After obtaining root access, they used custom Python scripts to scan the network, locate SMB resources, interact with SQL Server and WinRM, and access GitLab repositories for credentials and other sensitive data. Cisco released fixes on October 21, 2026, and users are advised to update supported versions, investigate for the published indicators of compromise, isolate affected systems, and limit lateral movement.

  • The exploitation was observed shortly after a public proof-of-concept was released, showing that public exploit code was followed quickly by real-world use against exposed Cisco Expressway devices.
  • Compromising an internet-facing Expressway device enabled access to additional cluster nodes on the internal network, illustrating how device clustering can extend the impact beyond the initially exposed systems.
  • Organizations can hunt for this activity using the published indicators, including "wombat@127.0.0.1" in Expressway Erlang logs and Python files staged under the specified /mnt/harddisk paths.
  • The attackers’ post-compromise scripts targeted SMB shares, SQL Server, WinRM, and GitLab repositories, so investigating an affected device should include checking those internal resources for follow-on activity and credential exposure.
Key Points
  • 01Threat actors exploited CVE-2026-76466, a Cisco Expressway vulnerability rated 9.8 out of 10, to run commands with the highest level of system access on affected devices.
  • 02F6 reported the apparent first observed real-world exploitation after a public proof-of-concept became available, affecting Cisco Expressway X15.5.3 devices at a Russian organization.
  • 03The attackers initially compromised two internet-facing Cisco Expressway devices and used one to reach two additional cluster nodes on the organization’s internal network.
  • 04After gaining access, the attackers used custom Python scripts to scan the network, identify accessible SMB resources, interact with SQL Server and WinRM, and access GitLab repositories to obtain credentials and sensitive data.
  • 05Cisco released fixes on October 21, 2026, with Expressway X15.5.20 addressing affected X15.5.3 and earlier releases.

    How Cloudflare WAF helps protect against phpAfterShell and other critical PHP flaws
    blog.cloudflare.com · 20 Nov 2026 20:00 UTC openai-codex / gpt-5.6-terra
    TAGScisacloudflarecve-2026-115560cve-2026-126714cve-2026-129289cve-2026-129474cve-2026-129481cve-2026-129496depthfirstfastcgi-request-smugglingphpphp-projectphpaftershellsession-deserializationsession-upload-progress
    In plain words

    PHP, a widely used tool for running websites, fixed a serious flaw called phpAfterShell that could let an outsider take control of a website’s server under certain conditions. Websites using older PHP versions, including sites built with content-management systems, plugins, or outdated container images, may be affected until their operators update and restart PHP. Cloudflare has added protections that can block known attempts to abuse the flaw, but those protections cannot see every route an attacker might use, so installing the PHP updates remains essential. The release also fixes six other critical PHP problems, raising the risk for organizations that delay updates.

    Summary
    Cloudflare updated its WAF to block known phpAfterShell exploit patterns by default, but organizations must urgently upgrade PHP to patched releases and restart all workers because the WAF cannot cover every exploitation path. The November 2026 PHP release fixes phpAfterShell and six other critical flaws, with additional Cloudflare rules available for PHP-FPM and SOAP issues.

    PHP fixed phpAfterShell (CVE-2026-126714), a critical vulnerability in its default file-based session handler that can lead to remote code execution, in releases published on November 19, 2026. The same releases also fixed 16 other security issues, including six additional critical flaws affecting components such as PHP-FPM, session handling, timezone caching, and fatal-error backtraces. The article states that there was no indication of exploitation in the wild as of November 19, and none of the 17 flaws was listed in CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.

    phpAfterShell can occur when a PHP session-file write is interrupted, leaving mixed old and new session data that PHP may later read as attacker-controlled objects. Exploitation can require a way to place controlled data into a session, an interruption at the right point during writing, and a suitable path to run code. Cloudflare updated an existing managed WAF rule to block known phpAfterShell patterns by default for all plans, while adding three paid-plan rules for PHP-FPM and SOAP flaws in logging mode. Cloudflare emphasizes that WAF coverage is only an additional layer of protection and that organizations should upgrade PHP, restart all workers, and apply temporary configuration mitigations if they cannot patch immediately.

    • Cloudflare’s existing PHP remote-code-execution rule detected part of the phpAfterShell technique before the flaw was publicly disclosed because phpAfterShell and the earlier php2shell issues both involve placing serialized data into session storage.
    • The final phpAfterShell trigger occurs when PHP later reads a corrupted session file, so a WAF can block malicious requests that place the payload but cannot block that internal read step itself.
    • The three new rules for PHP-FPM and SOAP flaws default to logging rather than blocking because their request patterns can also occur in legitimate traffic, requiring customers to review matches before enforcing blocks.
    • Several of the other critical PHP flaws require particular configurations, such as reused FastCGI connections, enabled upload-progress sessions, file-based error logging, or fatal-error backtraces, meaning exposure can differ substantially between deployments.
    • Linux distributions may backport PHP fixes without changing the visible PHP version number, so administrators need to compare their full package version with their distribution’s advisory rather than relying only on the PHP version label.
    Key Points
    • 01PHP disclosed and fixed phpAfterShell (CVE-2026-126714), a critical flaw in its default file-based session handling that can lead to remote code execution, in releases issued on November 19, 2026.
    • 02Cloudflare updated a PHP remote code execution managed WAF rule to cover known phpAfterShell attack patterns; the rule is enabled by default and blocks traffic for Free, Pro, Business, and Enterprise customers.
    • 03The same PHP releases fixed 16 additional security issues, including six other critical flaws affecting PHP-FPM, session handling, timezone caching, and fatal-error backtraces under specific conditions.
    • 04Cloudflare added three paid-plan managed WAF rules for a PHP-FPM issue and two PHP SOAP issues, but set their default action to Log so customers can assess whether matching requests are legitimate before blocking them.
    • 05Cloudflare states that WAF protections are not a replacement for patching, and organizations should upgrade PHP, restart every worker, and apply interim configuration mitigations if they cannot update immediately.

Although no exploitation was reported as of publication, the article provides concrete affected versions, mitigations, and WAF coverage that security professionals responsible for PHP environments should act on promptly.

In plain words

PHP released updates for two serious flaws that could let an outsider take control of affected websites or servers without needing an account. The risk applies to certain PHP versions used by web applications, especially those that store user session information in files. A successful attack could expose application data, passwords, and other secrets available to the affected system, so organizations should update PHP promptly.

Summary
PHP patched two critical session-handling flaws, CVE-2026-115560 and CVE-2026-126714, that could enable unauthenticated remote code execution on affected servers. Upgrade to PHP 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, 8.5.13, or later immediately, and temporarily disable session upload progress if patching is delayed.

PHP released security updates on November 19, 2026, covering 17 advisories and 18 CVE identifiers, including seven Critical-severity issues. This article focuses on two Critical PHP session vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-115560 and CVE-2026-126714, each rated CVSS 4.0 9.2 by the PHP security team. Both could enable unauthenticated remote code execution on affected PHP web servers, potentially exposing application data, secrets, and credentials available to the PHP process.

CVE-2026-115560 involves a mismatch between PHP session serialization formats that can cause attacker-controlled session data to be treated as serialized object data. CVE-2026-126714 affects PHP’s built-in files session handler, which can leave old trailing data in a session file if an update is interrupted and later cause mixed data to be interpreted as serialized objects. PHP fixed both issues in versions 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, and 8.5.13; the article recommends upgrading immediately, restarting relevant services, and temporarily disabling session upload progress when patching is delayed.

  • Checking only the command-line PHP version is insufficient after patching; organizations should verify that internet-facing PHP workers were restarted or reloaded and are running the updated version.
  • For CVE-2026-115560, disabling session upload progress must occur in administrative configuration before request input is processed, because an application-level ini_set() change happens too late.
  • Using different session serialization settings across PHP-FPM pools, virtual hosts, applications, or command-line jobs that share session storage can create exposure, so those settings should be consistent or their session storage isolated.
  • Disabling upload progress may reduce an accessible path for CVE-2026-126714, but it does not fix the underlying session-file write problem.
  • Organizations changing session serialization formats should assess existing session files and consider expiring or migrating old session data to avoid reading records created in a different format.
Key Points
  • 01PHP released security updates on November 19, 2026, addressing 17 advisories covering 18 CVE identifiers, including seven critical-severity issues.
  • 02CVE-2026-115560 is a session serialization mismatch involving PHP session upload progress that can lead to object deserialization and remote code execution.
  • 03CVE-2026-126714 affects PHP's built-in files session handler, where interrupted writes can leave mixed session data that may later be interpreted as serialized objects.
  • 04Both vulnerabilities affect PHP 8.2.0 through 8.2.35, 8.3.0 through 8.3.36, 8.4.0 through 8.4.27, and 8.5.0 through 8.5.12.
  • 05PHP fixed both issues in versions 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, and 8.5.13, and the article states that no public exploit code or active exploitation had been identified at the time of writing.

MoldyRoost is a large malvertising operation that uses cloaked ads and hidden iPhone browser frames to silently deliver Coruna and DarkSword iOS exploit chains, potentially stealing crypto wallet seed phrases, keychain data, messages and photos. Researchers linked more than 480 ad domains across six sub-clusters and found leaked source code showing per-campaign attribution for stolen data.

MoldyRoost is a malvertising operation that buys programmatic ads and uses cloaked landing pages to attempt drive-by compromise of vulnerable iPhones when users tap an ad. Researchers linked more than 480 advertising domains, arranged in six sub-clusters, to campaigns observed in more than 47 countries between May 12 and November 17, 2026. The operation is distinct from the November 16 Optimizely supply-chain attack, although both used Coruna and DarkSword iOS exploit kits and related version-routing infrastructure.

The campaigns show benign or decoy pages to most visitors but serve hidden browser frames to targeted iPhone Safari users, where the frames identify the iOS version and select an exploit chain. MoldyRoost uses Coruna, SilkPath, DarkSword, and GhostWave branches; the reported payloads can target crypto wallet seed phrases, keychain data, messages, photos, Wi-Fi passwords, location history, and other device data. A source-code exposure on the sub-cluster F server ab124[.]live revealed code attributed to “nano,” including Coruna- and DarkSword-style components and a mechanism that creates separate payloads for each sales channel so stolen data can be attributed to the campaign that delivered it.

  • MoldyRoost's loaders account for iOS 26 Safari reporting a frozen "18_6" operating-system version in its user agent by checking alternative version fields, indicating the operators actively adapt their targeting logic to platform changes.
  • Sub-cluster A can automatically move victims from in-app browsers and other iPhone browsers into Safari after a failed or stalled attempt, then restart the hidden exploit process rather than relying on the victim to follow manual instructions.
  • The exposed Nano source code shows that separate payloads were built for each sales channel so stolen data could be attributed to the campaign that delivered the victim, supporting a structured, performance-tracked distribution model.
  • The fake Cloudflare-style check used by sub-cluster D does not ask victims to paste commands or install anything; its purpose is to keep them on the page while the hidden iPhone exploit attempt runs.
  • Although the six sub-clusters use different ad themes and landing pages, they switch among exploit kits at nearly the same iOS-version boundaries and share delivery and tracking components.

In plain words

Ruby disclosed a critical flaw called ruby2shell that can let attackers take control of some websites and applications by sending specially crafted requests. Default Ruby on Rails and classic Sinatra apps are affected before users even sign in, as are some self-hosted products including GitLab, GitHub Enterprise Server, Mastodon, OpenProject, Discourse, and Chatwoot. Cloudflare has added protections for its customers, but the real fix is updating Ruby because harmful requests can still reach systems through routes Cloudflare cannot see.

Summary
Cloudflare has deployed default-blocking WAF rules for ruby2shell (CVE-2026-132825), a critical Ruby string case-conversion flaw that can enable pre-authentication RCE in default Rails and Sinatra deployments. Organizations should still urgently upgrade to Ruby 3.3.14, 3.4.13, or 4.0.10, as WAF protection cannot cover traffic that bypasses Cloudflare or non-HTTP attack paths.

Ruby disclosed ruby2shell, CVE-2026-132825, on November 19, 2026, describing a critical heap buffer overflow in string case conversion that can achieve remote code execution in some situations. The issue affects Ruby versions 3.3.13 and earlier, 3.4.0 through 3.4.12, and 4.0.0 through 4.0.9; fixes are available in Ruby 3.3.14, 3.4.13, and 4.0.10. Default Ruby on Rails and classic-style Sinatra applications can be exposed before authentication, and affected Ruby versions were bundled in several self-hosted products, including GitLab, GitHub Enterprise Server, Mastodon, OpenProject, Discourse, and Chatwoot.

The flaw occurs when Ruby processes the German sharp s character in certain legacy single-byte encodings: its uppercase form is SS, but Ruby checks for space for only one byte before writing two. Rack’s MethodOverride middleware can trigger the vulnerable conversion while processing a specially formed multipart POST request’s _method value, before application code or authentication checks run. Cloudflare added default-blocking managed WAF rules for ruby2shell and the related GHSA-87fm-7w84-j2px integer overflow for all customers, including Free-plan users, but states that upgrading Ruby remains necessary because direct-to-origin traffic and non-HTTP inputs can bypass WAF coverage.

  • The flaw is triggered by the German sharp s character in certain legacy single-byte character sets, where Ruby reserves space for one byte but writes its two-character uppercase form, SS.
  • A multipart POST request can reach the vulnerable case-conversion code during request routing through Rack's _method handling, before an application’s authentication checks or application code run.
  • UTF-8 strings use a different Ruby code path and are not affected; the exposed path depends on legacy ISO-8859 and Windows-125x encodings.
  • Updating an application alone may not be sufficient when Ruby is bundled inside self-hosted products or container images; the article specifically recommends updating those products and rebuilding container images.
  • Cloudflare’s additional rule also covers GHSA-87fm-7w84-j2px, a separate integer overflow in the same Ruby string case-conversion code fixed in the same Ruby releases.
Key Points
  • 01Ruby disclosed ruby2shell (CVE-2026-132825) on November 19, 2026, a critical heap buffer overflow in string case conversion that Ruby says can lead to remote code execution in some scenarios.
  • 02Ruby 3.3.14, 3.4.13, and 4.0.10 contain fixes for ruby2shell, while Ruby 3.2 and earlier are end of life and will not receive the fix.
  • 03Default Ruby on Rails and classic-style Sinatra applications can reach the flaw before authentication through Rack's handling of the _method parameter in multipart POST requests.
  • 04Cloudflare added default-blocking ruby2shell and related GHSA-87fm-7w84-j2px managed WAF rules for customers, including those on its Free plan.
  • 05Cloudflare states that WAF rules are a temporary compensating control and recommends upgrading Ruby because direct-to-origin traffic and non-HTTP inputs can bypass WAF coverage.

JUSTIFICATION

This covers a newly disclosed critical Ruby flaw with reported remote-code-execution proof-of-concepts and a pre-authentication path in default Rails and Sinatra configurations. It affects widely used Ruby versions and self-hosted products, making prompt patching and temporary WAF coverage highly relevant.

Summary
Com-affiliated extortion groups, including Bling Libra and newly tracked Vortex and Cinder clusters, are using IT-support vishing and adversary-in-the-middle phishing to steal cloud credentials, enroll rogue MFA devices, exfiltrate Microsoft 365 data, and extort data-rich organizations. Defenses should prioritize phishing-resistant MFA, strict help-desk identity verification, browser-extension allowlisting, and monitoring for unauthorized identity and data-export activity.

Unit 42 reported sustained vishing-based data theft and extortion by Com-affiliated threat actors, including Bling Libra (ShinyHunters) and activity clusters Redact, Pink, Falcon, Helix, Vortex, and Cinder. The campaigns have primarily targeted data-rich financial services, healthcare, and legal organizations in the United States, United Kingdom, and Australia. Attackers impersonate internal IT support personnel and direct employees to organization-themed phishing sites designed to capture credentials and multi-factor authentication approvals. The article says this activity accelerated significantly around August 2026, with healthcare becoming the most targeted industry in September and October.

After gaining access, the actors commonly enroll unauthorized MFA devices, replay authenticated sessions, use residential proxies or commercial VPNs, and collect data through native cloud tools and scripted API access. Vortex was observed targeting Microsoft 365 mailboxes, OneDrive, and SharePoint, while Cinder used persistent session tokens and the Microsoft Graph SDK to collect SharePoint and OneDrive data. The actors then sent internal Microsoft Teams or email messages claiming data theft and directing employees to Tor-hosted negotiation sites. Unit 42 also identified a sideloaded browser extension masquerading as Google Chrome that could log keystrokes, steal authentication cookies and browser storage, capture QR-code login information, stream webcam feeds, and remotely control browsers.

The report emphasizes that these groups increasingly rely on data theft and extortion rather than encrypting victim systems, allowing them to move quickly while avoiding many custom tools. It recommends tighter help-desk verification, phishing-resistant MFA such as FIDO2 or passkeys, browser-extension allowlists, visibility into identity actions, and alerts on unauthorized data exports. Unit 42 published indicators including malicious browser-extension hashes, domains, IP addresses, device names, and user-agent strings associated with the activity.

  • Vortex operators enrolled an unauthorized MFA device within minutes of successful authentication and repeatedly used the same device name, "Pixel 10a," across compromised accounts.
  • Cinder operators avoided triggering new Duo MFA prompts by replaying a persistent "keep me signed in" session token from proxy infrastructure.
  • The identified browser extension was deliberately named "Google Chrome" to make Chrome’s developer-mode warning appear less suspicious, while giving operators capabilities including keylogging, webcam streaming, clipboard theft, screenshots, and remote browser control.
  • Com-affiliated infrastructure used short-lived, target-specific subdomains on domains themed around SSO, MFA, passkeys, IT support, reports, and claims, sometimes with Cloudflare Pages redirects to organization-specific phishing pages.

In plain words

Researchers found a flaw in Linux’s KVM software that allowed someone controlling a virtual computer on certain AMD-based servers to access the physical server’s memory. On shared cloud servers, that memory could contain information belonging to other customers, meaning one customer’s virtual machine could potentially see or alter data it should never reach. The issue affects servers that allow virtual computers to run additional virtual computers, and providers and server owners need to update the main server software or turn that feature off.

Summary
CVE-2026-99312 is a critical AMD-specific Linux KVM nested-virtualization flaw that can let a root-controlled guest VM read, and potentially write, host memory. Cloud and KVM operators should install the fixed host kernel and reboot, or disable nested virtualization until patching is complete.

Researchers disclosed CVE-2026-99312, an AMD-specific flaw in Linux KVM that can allow a guest virtual machine with root access to access host memory when nested virtualization is enabled. In testing on a DigitalOcean Droplet, they read roughly 127 GB of host RAM, including the host kernel version banner. On a separate bare-metal AMD system, they wrote 32 selected bytes into a live host-kernel memory page. DigitalOcean patched its fleet with a live patch and said customers did not need to take action.

The issue affects AMD KVM hosts with nested virtualization enabled, while Intel-based KVM hosts are not affected. It stems from KVM leaving a memory-management pointer directed at freed memory after an INIT reset stops a nested virtual machine. If that page is reused, a guest can populate it with crafted translation entries that reference physical memory on the host. The fix resets this KVM memory-management state during every INIT.

Fixed kernels are available upstream in stable kernel 7.3.5 and long-term kernels 6.18.64 and 6.12.118, but the article says several distribution kernels had not yet received fixes at publication. Updating virtual machines themselves does not address the problem because the affected code is in the host kernel, and hosts require a reboot after installing a fixed kernel. Until patching is complete, operators can disable nested virtualization, though doing so prevents virtual machines from running virtual machines of their own.

  • The vulnerable code was introduced by a 2022 security fix for CVE-2022-3344, illustrating that a patch for one nested-virtualization problem created another flaw that remained for nearly four years.
  • Updating a guest VM does not mitigate this issue because the vulnerable component runs in the host kernel; even after installing a fixed host kernel, the host must be rebooted for protection to take effect.
  • Nested virtualization is enabled by default in the kvm_amd module according to VirtFusion, so an unpatched AMD KVM host may be exposed unless an operator intentionally changed that setting.
  • There is no published exploit code, no reported exploitation outside research, and no available guidance for determining whether an attempted exploitation occurred.
  • Severity assessments differ substantially: the Linux kernel CVE team assigned an 8.8 score, Red Hat initially categorized it as Moderate at 5.6 with denial-of-service impact, and DigitalOcean treated it as critical in its shared-cloud environment.
Key Points
  • 01CVE-2026-99312 is an AMD-specific Linux KVM flaw involving nested virtualization that allowed researchers with root access in a guest VM to read approximately 127 GB of host memory on a DigitalOcean server.
  • 02On their own bare-metal AMD server, the researchers also wrote 32 selected bytes into a live host-kernel memory page, and a kernel module confirmed the modification.
  • 03The flaw occurs when an INIT reset for a nested VM leaves KVM using a pointer to freed memory, allowing a guest to forge memory-translation entries that can reference host physical memory.
  • 04Upstream fixes reset KVM’s memory-management state during every INIT and were released in stable kernel 7.3.5 and long-term kernels 6.18.64 and 6.12.118.
  • 05Operators should update and reboot vulnerable AMD KVM hosts, or disable nested virtualization with the kvm_amd nested=0 setting until they can install a fixed kernel.

JUSTIFICATION

This is a high-impact, concrete KVM host-isolation flaw that can allow a root-controlled guest VM on vulnerable AMD systems to read host memory and demonstrated limited host-kernel writes. It is especially important to cloud and virtualization operators because nested virtualization is reportedly enabled by default and mitigation requires a host-kernel update and reboot or disabling the feature.

The operators supplied IP addresses and asked the tool to obtain shell access, after which its AI agents planned, executed, and adjusted actions without the operator choosing every next step.     Amazon said the agents discovered and exploited an unpatched path traversal flaw in the open-source MONAI Label medical-imaging AI application, assessing with high confidence that it was a zero-day because no prior fix, issue, advisory, or database entry existed. The apparent zero-day was then used to breach a second university, and the Project MONAI maintainers fixed the flaw after Amazon contacted them. Although several efforts failed, including a 16-hour attempt involving 148 actions and another that tested more than 30,000 credential combinations, Amazon said the campaign showed AI agents can operate continuously and move faster than many security operations centers can manually triage alerts.

    • Amazon assessed the MONAI Label flaw as an apparent zero-day because it found no prior fix, issue, advisory, or vulnerability-database reference for the path traversal problem at the time it was discovered.

In plain words

Amazon researchers say suspected China-linked hackers used Cairn, a tool that lets artificial-intelligence programs work on hacking tasks independently, to find an unknown weakness in MONAI Label medical-imaging software and take full control of a server. The campaign mainly targeted educational institutions in East Asia, and the attackers then tried to use access to one university network to reach other machines running the same software. The software makers released an update after Amazon reported the problem. The case matters because AI tools may help attackers find and use software weaknesses faster than people can investigate and fix them.

Summary
Amazon Threat Intelligence says a suspected Chinese-linked actor used the autonomous AI platform Cairn to discover and exploit a path traversal zero-day in MONAI Label, gaining root access to a server within minutes. MONAI patched the flaw on November 18, highlighting how AI agents can accelerate vulnerability discovery and exploitation.

Amazon Threat Intelligence reported that a suspected Chinese-nexus threat actor used the autonomous AI agent platform Cairn to discover and exploit a zero-day flaw in MONAI Label, an open-source medical-imaging application. The attackers reportedly instructed the agents to obtain shell access, while the agents independently mapped the application and found a path traversal issue. The activity occurred between September 8 and 10, 2026, and mainly targeted educational institutions in East Asia outside China. Amazon attributed the campaign with moderate confidence based on retrieved prompt language, activity timing, and target selection.

The MONAI Label flaw allowed files to be written to arbitrary locations on a server, and Amazon said the agents moved from API mapping to exploitation within 11 minutes. In a later session, they wrote a Python reverse shell into sitecustomize.py, which loads when Python starts, then triggered an API endpoint to obtain root access. Afterward, the operator supplied a proxy into another university network using the same vulnerable software and directed the agents to target additional machines. Project MONAI released a security update after Amazon reported the flaw.

The campaign also showed that the agents did not always succeed: an attempt to take over a Redis server failed after 16 hours and 148 actions, and a six-hour attempt involving more than 30,000 credential combinations against a university GPU server also failed. Amazon found the operation after the attackers left a Cairn instance publicly reachable without authentication. The researchers warned that AI agents can find and use software flaws faster than security teams can react and urged organizations to make greater use of automated defenses.

  • The attackers’ publicly accessible, unauthenticated Cairn instance exposed their operations and enabled Amazon Threat Intelligence to investigate the campaign.
  • The AI agents mapped MONAI Label’s API and exploited the path traversal flaw within 11 minutes, illustrating a short interval between identifying an application and obtaining a usable path to server compromise.
  • Cairn’s automation was not consistently successful: a 16-hour, 148-action attempt against Redis failed, as did a six-hour effort involving more than 30,000 credential combinations against a university GPU server.
  • After finding the MONAI Label flaw, the operator supplied access to a second university network running the same software and directed the agents to pursue additional machines.
Key Points
  • 01Amazon Threat Intelligence reported that a suspected Chinese-linked threat actor used the autonomous AI agent platform Cairn to seek shell access to targeted servers.
  • 02Cairn agents found and exploited a path traversal zero-day in MONAI Label, allowing arbitrary file writes and leading to root access through a Python reverse shell placed in sitecustomize.py.
  • 03Amazon said the campaign occurred between September 8 and 10, 2026, mainly targeting East Asian educational institutions outside China.
  • 04MONAI Label maintainers released a security update for the reported flaw on November 18.
  • 05Amazon warned that AI agents can discover and exploit weaknesses faster than security teams can respond, and urged greater reliance on automated defenses.

The RAT can remotely control desktops, stream screens, capture microphone and camera data, manage files, perform system reconnaissance, and run additional payloads, communicating with attacker-controlled infrastructure using DNS over HTTPS.   • Behavior-based monitoring can identify misuse of a trusted integration by detecting first-seen networks or user agents, unexpected hosting or VPN infrastructure, and unusually large data reads.

A newly disclosed, unpatched Windows zero-day technique called FastUnlock can allow someone with physical access to a locked computer to start programs without signing in. The method was published by a researcher known as MSNightmare or Nightmare Eclipse, and ThreatLocker said it independently tested and confirmed it works. No Microsoft fix has been released, and the article says there is no evidence that the technique has been used in real attacks.

FastUnlock requires physical access, a Microsoft account reachable through lock-screen recovery options, and use of Windows Narrator to navigate the locked screen. ThreatLocker reached a point where it could run a program under WSIAccount, which it identified as a limited, non-administrator account. BitLocker systems that automatically unlock drives through the TPM may still be exposed because the drive is already unlocked by the time the lock screen appears; the article recommends stronger physical controls, a BitLocker startup PIN, and shutting down or hibernating sensitive devices.

  • A standard BitLocker setup that unlocks the drive automatically with the computer’s security chip may not stop this method, because the drive is already available by the time the lock screen appears.
  • Adding a BitLocker startup PIN is only protective before the computer starts, so it does not help if the device is already running and sitting at its lock screen.
  • The disclosed method does not defeat disk encryption or provide administrator access; it operates after the system has already unlocked its own drive and reaches a limited account.
  • The original disclosure contains little written detail, while ThreatLocker’s independent test provides the clearest description of the technique’s practical effect.

  • 04BitLocker configurations that automatically unlock drives through the TPM may not prevent FastUnlock because the drive is already unlocked when the lock screen appears.

In plain words

Researchers found two Android phone threats, Bazuka and ArcticRAT, that can disguise themselves as familiar apps and trick people into installing them. Once on a phone, they can watch what a person types, steal bank details and verification codes, read messages, replace cryptocurrency payment addresses, and let criminals control the device while hiding what is happening on screen. This matters because infected users could lose money, private information, and control of their phones without realizing it.

Researchers uncovered Bazuka, a modular Android banking-malware framework that uses deceptive screen overlays, keylogging, NFC and SMS/2FA interception, ADB-based device control, and AI-assisted victim targeting. A separate Android RAT, ArcticRAT, similarly uses LLMs and black-screen overlays to steal financial data and remotely control infected devices.

ThreatFabric disclosed Bazuka, a previously unknown Android malware framework discovered during an investigation in late October 2026. The framework consists of a dropper or downloader, a core component, and 23 modules supporting functions such as fake login screens, keystroke capture, SMS and verification-code interception, remote control, and cryptocurrency-address replacement. Its control panel also integrates large language models that operators can use to identify and score victims.

Bazuka can capture an image of a phone’s home or lock screen and show it as a cover while malicious actions occur behind it. Its core can use Android accessibility features and Wireless Debugging to gain additional control, while communicating with its operators through separate WebSocket channels for commands and stolen data. The article also highlights ArcticRAT, another Android remote-access tool that uses language-model APIs to identify valuable financial information in stolen data and black-screen overlays to conceal activity from victims.

  • Bazuka can use Android accessibility features to open settings, enable Wireless Debugging, capture its pairing PIN, and connect to the device’s Android debugging service, allowing it to seek additional control without relying solely on its original app permissions.
  • Both Bazuka and ArcticRAT conceal attacker activity from the phone owner through screen manipulation: Bazuka displays a captured image of the home or lock screen, while ArcticRAT uses an unclosable black screen and reduces brightness to zero.
  • Bazuka’s builders can select permissions for each dropper app, a design that ThreatFabric said is likely intended to help evade Google Play review, while its distribution model also supports criminals who drive installs through ads or fraudulent websites.
  • ArcticRAT uses a VPN privilege to block network communications on the compromised phone during staging, which Zimperium said can blind Google Play Protect telemetry.

In plain words

A fake website claims to offer a way to stream GTA VI on a Windows computer, then tells visitors to paste and run a command that secretly installs harmful software. People who follow those instructions can have saved browser passwords, gaming accounts, cryptocurrency wallet information, and other private data stolen. This matters because the scam uses the popularity of a game that is not officially available for PC to make a dangerous step look like a normal installation.

Summary
A fake GTA VI PC streaming client uses a ClickFix lure to persuade Windows users to run a PowerShell command that installs an information-stealing malware payload. Anyone who ran it should treat the device as compromised, scan it, and change important passwords from a clean device.

Bitdefender researchers identified a fake GTA VI PC streaming website that tells Windows users to press Win+R and run a pasted PowerShell command. The command downloads a ZIP archive, unpacks it into AppData, and starts GTA6Cloud.exe. The site presents this as a way to stream GTA VI from a PlayStation or Xbox console rather than download the game itself, while stating it is unaffiliated with Rockstar Games or Take-Two Interactive.

GTA6Cloud.exe displays a GTA VI-themed decoy page and trailer while downloading additional files, including loadperf.dll and the legitimate Windows utility unlodctr.exe, into a hidden folder. The attackers use the legitimate utility to load the malicious DLL, which injects a Rust-based information stealer into legitimate Windows processes. The stealer can collect browser credentials, cookies, tokens, gaming and cryptocurrency wallet data, AI and developer-service credentials, clipboard contents, and screenshots, and can send stolen information to its command-and-control infrastructure.

The article describes the scheme as a ClickFix attack because victims are convinced to run the command themselves rather than the attackers exploiting a software flaw. Users who ran the command are advised to treat the computer as compromised, disconnect it from the internet if possible, scan it with trusted security software, and change important passwords from a separate clean device. Users who only visited the site without running the command or opening a downloaded file did not complete the described installation chain.

  • The scam avoids the implausible claim of offering a downloadable GTA VI PC game and instead presents itself as a client for streaming the game from a PlayStation or Xbox console.
  • The PowerShell instruction uses both an execution-policy bypass and a command that immediately runs internet-downloaded code, so users are asked to execute code without reviewing it first.
  • The malicious DLL is designed to forward most functions to a legitimate Windows component so that the legitimate host program continues working while the malware runs.
  • Simply visiting the malicious site does not complete the described infection chain; the user must run the pasted command or open the downloaded file.
Key Points
  • 01A fake GTA VI PC streaming website instructs Windows users to use Win+R to run a PowerShell command that downloads and starts GTA6Cloud.exe.
  • 02The downloaded executable displays a GTA VI-themed decoy while downloading additional files, including loadperf.dll and unlodctr.exe, into a hidden folder.
  • 03The malware abuses the legitimate Windows program unlodctr.exe to load its malicious DLL and injects a Rust-based information stealer into legitimate Windows processes.
  • 04The stealer can collect browser credentials, cookies, tokens, Discord and Steam data, cryptocurrency wallet data, AI and developer-service credentials, clipboard contents, and screenshots.
  • 05People who ran the command should treat the computer as compromised, disconnect it from the internet, scan it with trusted security software, and change important passwords from a clean device.

In plain words

The United States and European Union have announced new programs to help hospitals and other healthcare providers better protect themselves from digital threats. In South Carolina, Project Lifeline 250 will connect rural hospitals with government and technology companies that can help find weaknesses and reduce disruption from computer attacks. Across Europe, seven funded projects will help healthcare organizations assess risks, train staff, improve monitoring, and maintain patient care after an incident. These efforts matter because successful attacks on healthcare can interrupt services that people rely on for treatment and care.

Summary
The United States and European Union have launched new health-sector cybersecurity initiatives: South Carolina’s Project Lifeline 250 will provide rural hospitals with free public-private security support, while the EU is funding seven projects to improve hospital resilience, monitoring, training, and NIS2 compliance.

The United States and European Union have announced new initiatives intended to strengthen cybersecurity in the health sector. In the United States, the White House Office of the National Cyber Director and South Carolina launched Project Lifeline 250, a six-month pilot focused on rural hospitals. The program connects participating hospitals with government and private-sector organizations that can provide tools and services to identify weaknesses, improve security, and reduce disruptions from cyberattacks.

Project Lifeline 250 follows Project Watershed 250, a similar Texas pilot for the water sector that pairs federal and private-sector capabilities with state and local expertise at no cost to participants. Microsoft, Trellix, Zscaler, and Cisco are among the technology companies participating in the South Carolina effort. In Europe, the European Commission and European Cybersecurity Competence Centre announced seven Digital Europe Programme-funded projects covering risk and maturity assessments, staff training, AI-driven cybersecurity tools, continuity of care, recovery, and support for NIS2 compliance.

  • The U.S. approach is a time-limited, state-based pilot focused specifically on rural hospitals, using federal, state, and private-sector support at no cost to participating organizations.
  • Project Lifeline 250 follows the same model as Texas’s Project Watershed 250, indicating that the White House is testing a reusable approach across different critical-infrastructure sectors.

In plain words

The article examines PHP2Shell, two serious flaws in PHP, a common tool used to run websites, that were disclosed and then actively abused within days. Government agencies, schools, local authorities, and organizations using websites or commercial products built with affected PHP versions may be at risk, including when they do not realize PHP is running behind the scenes. It matters because attackers can use an exposed website or network device as a way into an organization, then potentially reach more sensitive systems and accounts. The article argues that organizations need an up-to-date picture of their internet-facing systems and a plan to quickly fix or temporarily disconnect affected services.

Summary
PHP2Shell illustrates how quickly critical runtime vulnerabilities can progress from disclosure to active exploitation, making continuous asset visibility and risk-based remediation essential for public-sector organizations. Agencies should identify internet-exposed PHP and related systems in advance, prioritize actively exploited flaws, and limit post-compromise paths to root access, management infrastructure, and directory services.

PHP2Shell refers to two critical PHP runtime vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, that can allow unauthenticated remote code execution on affected web servers. Details leaked before their planned disclosure, PHP maintainers released emergency fixes on October 21, and CISA confirmed active exploitation within days before adding both flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. The article says the rapid transition from disclosure to exploitation demonstrated how quickly organizations may need to respond to broadly affecting runtime flaws.

Public-sector agencies, including federal, state, local, and education organizations, may have difficulty finding affected systems because PHP can operate beneath websites, content management systems, commercial products, and cloud workloads. The article recommends continuously identifying where PHP and other runtimes are used, prioritizing systems based on active exploitation evidence, internet exposure, KEV status, and exploit prediction information rather than severity scores alone. It also highlights reported attacks in which PHP2Shell gave attackers low-privilege code execution and the Fragnesia Linux kernel flaw, CVE-2026-46300, was used to obtain root access, underscoring the need to restrict what internet-facing systems can reach inside an organization.

  • A runtime-level flaw can expose an organization even when its own application code has no major weakness, because PHP may be embedded beneath a website, content management system, plugin, or commercial product.
  • The article notes that about 59% of internet-facing PHP hosts were running end-of-life branches, making legacy software a major obstacle to rapid remediation.
  • In reported PAN-OS compromises, PHP2Shell reportedly provided low-privilege code execution while the Fragnesia Linux kernel flaw was used to obtain root access, showing why fixing only the initial entry flaw may leave a dangerous escalation path.
  • Network appliances that share the same build present an unusually broad risk because a single exploit tuned for that build can work against every exposed, unpatched device running it.
  • CVE-2026-115560 demonstrates that version inventory alone may not be enough, because whether it is exploitable also depends on session settings and the libraries an application uses.
Key Points
  • 01PHP2Shell consists of CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, critical PHP runtime flaws that can allow unauthenticated remote code execution on affected web servers.
  • 02PHP maintainers released emergency patches on October 21 after details leaked, and CISA later added both flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog after confirming active exploitation.
  • 03Public-sector organizations may struggle to identify affected systems because PHP can run beneath websites, content management systems, commercial products, and cloud workloads without being obvious to security teams.
  • 04The article recommends prioritizing remediation using active-exploitation evidence, internet exposure, KEV status, and exploit prediction scores rather than CVSS severity alone.
  • 05The article advises organizations to reduce the impact of an initial breach by patching kernels, restricting unprivileged user namespaces, and limiting edge devices' access to management networks, directory services, and stored credentials.

The Path to AI Autonomy in the SOC

TAGSa16zai-socgartnerintezermcpowaspuniversity-of-washington

In plain words

The article explains how companies can let AI assistants help their security teams investigate warnings and, in some cases, take limited actions on their own. Many security leaders expect to give these tools more freedom soon because human analysts are overwhelmed, but they remain cautious about actions that could interrupt employees or important business systems. The article argues that companies should start with low-risk tasks, require clear proof before approving bigger actions, and treat each AI assistant like a powerful employee account that must be closely limited and monitored.

Summary
SOC teams should grant AI agents autonomy incrementally by action type, automating low-risk investigation tasks first while requiring evidence, approval, and rollback plans for disruptive responses. Treat AI agents as privileged identities and expand or reduce their authority based on measured performance, auditability, and blast radius.

Security leaders are increasingly considering AI agents for security operations, with an a16z survey finding that 36% of CISOs are currently comfortable with autonomous low-risk actions and 60% expect to be comfortable within 12 months. The article argues that autonomy should not be treated as a single choice between suggestions and fully independent action. Instead, AI authority should differ across evidence gathering, analysis, response recommendations, and actions that change an organization’s systems.

The article recommends granting autonomy according to whether an action can be reversed, how widely it could affect users or systems, and how strong the supporting evidence is. Read-only log queries and indicator enrichment can be fully automated, while actions such as disabling accounts or isolating production servers should retain human approval or direction. Teams should set measurable criteria for increasing or reducing autonomy, test new actions without making real changes, preserve complete evidence trails, and ensure rollback procedures exist.

Human approval is meaningful only when reviewers receive enough evidence to quickly verify the agent’s conclusion rather than merely approving requests to keep work moving. The article also advises treating an AI SOC agent as a privileged identity with its own credentials, narrowly scoped permissions, complete logging, and monitoring. This is important because greater autonomy can increase the damage an agent could cause if it is incorrect, manipulated, or compromised.

  • Human approval can become ineffective when reviewers receive too little context and begin approving requests simply to keep work moving; the article suggests that a reviewer should be able to verify a verdict within one or two minutes.
  • An AI agent’s technical capability should not determine its authority by itself, because an agent can be highly capable while still operating under close human direction when the consequences demand it.
  • Autonomy should be reduced as well as expanded: falling agreement rates, major environment changes, or a serious mistake should trigger a lower level of authority until the agent again meets predefined criteria.
  • Testing proposed response actions in a mode that simulates every system-changing step lets teams observe what an agent would have done before permitting it to make actual changes.
  • The same authority that enables a SOC agent to respond also increases the harm it could cause if it is wrong, manipulated, or compromised, so its permissions should be limited to its approved tasks.
Key Points
  • 01A recent a16z survey found that 36% of CISOs at organizations with more than 1,000 employees are currently comfortable allowing AI agents to autonomously take low-risk security actions, rising to 60% within 12 months.
  • 02The article separates AI SOC work into evidence collection, analysis and verdicts, response recommendations, and response execution, arguing that each stage can have a different level of autonomy.
  • 03The article recommends deciding an AI agent's autonomy for each action based on reversibility, the number of people or systems affected, and the strength of verifiable evidence supporting the decision.
  • 04For higher-impact response actions, approval requests should include the collected evidence, the reasoning linking it to the conclusion, and checks the agent performed to rule out alternatives.
  • 05The article recommends treating a SOC AI agent as a privileged identity by giving it its own credentials, limiting its permissions, logging its tool use and actions, and monitoring it.
